summary: This memo identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet, with comments on planned changes. It updates and obsoletes RFC 944 and was replaced by RFC 991.

plainLanguage.summary: A refreshed checklist of the official network rulebooks. A newer one soon took its place.

questions: what were the official internet protocols in late 1985
which internet protocols were required vs elective
where is the internet protocol status report
subtitle: A status report on the official Internet protocols and their implementation status in late 1985.

tldr.problem: The Internet community needed to know which protocols were official, required, recommended, elective, or experimental, along with their specifications and implementation status.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 961 provides a comprehensive list of all official protocols, organized by network level (IP, ICMP, UDP, TCP), host level (HMP, EGP, GGP), and application level (Telnet, FTP, SMTP, Domain, etc.), with status, specification, and contact information for each.
tldr.outcome: This reference document was quickly superseded by RFC 991 in late 1986, which consolidated protocol information with a similar structure but updated status.

today: RFC 961 has been obsoleted by RFC 991, published in November 1986, which consolidated and updated the protocol status information. RFC 961 remains a historical reference documenting the state of Internet protocols at the end of 1985.

sections.title: Introduction and Protocol Classification
sections.content: RFC 961 is an official status report documenting the protocols in use in the ARPA-Internet community in December 1985. The document identifies protocol specifications and provides comments on planned changes and implementation status. Protocols are classified into four categories: required (all hosts must implement), recommended (hosts are encouraged to implement), elective (hosts may or may not implement), and experimental (only for participating experiments with contact coordination). This classification scheme helps implementers understand which protocols are mandatory for Internet participation.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sorts all Internet protocols into four boxes: must have, should have, may have, and experimental. This makes it clear which rules are mandatory and which are optional.

sections.title: Network Layer Protocols
sections.content: At the network layer, the RFC identifies three core protocols. The Internet Protocol (IP) defined in RFC 791 is marked as required and is the universal protocol providing datagram delivery and host addressing. The document notes confusion in the route options specification and mentions ICMP as an integral part of IP that must be implemented. The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), defined in RFC 792, is also required and provides control messages and error reporting alongside IP. The User Datagram Protocol (UDP) is recommended and provides datagram service to applications at the host level, adding port addressing to IP services. Several experimental protocols are also covered, including the Gateway Gateway Protocol (GGP), Multiplexing Protocol (MUX), Stream Protocol (ST), and others, along with address resolution protocols like ARP and RARP.
sections.plainLanguage: IP is like the addressing system that makes sure data gets to the right computer. ICMP sends error messages when something goes wrong. UDP lets programs send quick messages without waiting for a reply. Some other protocols were being tested but not yet approved for general use.

sections.title: Host Level and Transport Protocols
sections.content: The host level covers UDP (described above) and the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), defined in RFC 793 and marked as recommended. TCP provides reliable end-to-end data stream service. The RFC documents numerous corrections and clarifications needed in the TCP specification, including issues with the event processing section, the push flag semantics, the urgent pointer definition, listening servers, maximum segment size negotiation, idle connection handling, and out-of-order segment processing. The RFC also covers the Host Monitoring Protocol (HMP), Cross Net Debugger (XNET), and experimental protocols like Reliable Data Protocol (RDP), Multiplexing Protocol, Stream Protocol, Network Voice Protocol, and Internet Reliable Transaction Protocol (IRTP).
sections.plainLanguage: TCP is like ordering mail with proof of delivery, while UDP is like a postcard. TCP makes sure everything arrives and in order; UDP is faster but does not promise anything. The document lists many issues in how TCP was written that needed fixing.

sections.title: Application Level Protocols
sections.content: The application layer contains the most protocols. Telnet (RFC 854) is recommended for remote terminal access, with numerous options documented. The File Transfer Protocol (FTP) (RFC 959) is recommended for moving files between hosts, with new optional commands like CDUP, SMNT, STOU, RMD, MKD, and PWD. Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) (RFC 821) is recommended for transmitting mail between hosts. The Domain Name System (RFCs 881, 882, 883) is recommended and uses TCP or UDP. Other protocols include Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP), Simple File Transfer Protocol (SFTP), Resource Location Protocol (RLP), Remote Job Entry (RJE), debugging protocols (Echo, Discard, Chargen), information protocols (Quote of the Day, Users, Finger, WhoIs), time protocols (Daytime, Network Time Protocol, Time Server), and experimental protocols like Post Office Protocol Version 2, Message Processing Module (MPM), and Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP).
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet lets you use a remote computer like it is sitting in front of you. FTP moves files between computers. SMTP sends email between mail servers. DNS looks up addresses. There are also simple tools like the echo service and time servers, plus experimental ones that people were trying out.

sections.title: Implementation Notes and Status
sections.content: The RFC provides implementation guidance throughout. IP implementations must include ICMP. The TCP specification, while recommended, has numerous documented issues requiring careful interpretation by implementers. The RFC notes that some protocols were revised since earlier versions in the Internet Protocol Transition Workbook (IPTW), particularly mail protocols (revised as a November 1982 volume), Telnet and options (June 1983 volume), and FTP (RFC 959, most recent at that time). The document identifies contact people for each protocol and references related implementation guides such as RFC 815 on IP datagram reassembly and RFC 819 on the names, addresses, ports, and routes. The RFC also covers protocols for network interconnection, including the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP), Internet Protocol on various networks (X.25, DC, Ethernet, IEEE 802.3), and Internet subnetting (RFC 950). The appendices address service mappings, address mappings, document formats, bitmap formats, and facsimile formats.
sections.plainLanguage: The document tells implementers which protocols depend on each other, where to find specifications, and who to contact with questions. It lists all the problems in existing protocols that people knew about. Some protocols were revisions of older ones, and the document keeps track of which versions are current.
